screens.title: Who waited
screens.prose: A test client sends one request, waits for the reply, then sends the next. Requests should go out every 100 µs. One reply took 50 ms, and requests due meanwhile waited behind it. Two reports measure 2,000 requests.
screens.question: Which report shows what a request queued behind the stall felt?

options.text: Done minus intended: the time since it should have gone
Done minus sent: the time since the client actually sent it
options.why: The client sent late because it was waiting. That wait is missing from this report.

options.text: They are the same measure
options.why: They differ by exactly the time each request waited to be sent.

options.text: Neither: one stall is just noise
options.why: Delayed requests number 875 of 2,000, far more than one.

hints.text: A queued request was due earlier than it was sent.
Which clock starts when the request should have gone?
Done minus intended counts the wait. Done minus sent hides it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which report starts the clock at the due time?

byKey.sent: You picked the report that starts after the wait.
byKey.same: The gap between them is the queueing time.
byKey.noise: 875 requests were late by over 100 µs. That is not one outlier.

explain.text: The client held back the requests due in the stall, so done minus sent shows only 50 µs at p99. Done minus intended starts at the due time and shows 48,821 µs. Waiting for each reply hides the delay: coordinated omission.

screens.title: Measure it both ways
screens.prose: `latencies.csv` holds the run: one row per request with its intended, sent and done times in µs. Rank is the position in the sorted list, counted from 1.
screens.question: Fix `report` so it returns both sets of percentiles and the true mean.

widget.starter:
import csv

def report(path):
    """Read latencies.csv (seq, intended_us, sent_us, done_us). A closed-loop client sent each request
    when the previous reply arrived. Return nearest-rank percentiles (rank = ceil(p * n / 100)) of
    done - sent ("sent") and of done - intended ("true"), and the mean of the true latency."""
    with open(path) as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    sent = sorted(int(r["done_us"]) - int(r["sent_us"]) for r in rows)
    mid = sent[len(sent) // 2]
    return {"p50_sent": mid, "p99_sent": mid, "p999_sent": mid,
            "p50_true": mid, "p99_true": mid, "p999_true": mid,
            "mean_true": sum(sent) / len(sent)}
widget.solution:
import csv

def nearest_rank(values, permille):
    s = sorted(values)
    rank = max(1, -(-permille * len(s) // 1000))      # ceil(permille * n / 1000) in integers
    return s[rank - 1]

def report(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    sent = [int(r["done_us"]) - int(r["sent_us"]) for r in rows]
    true = [int(r["done_us"]) - int(r["intended_us"]) for r in rows]
    return {
        "p50_sent": nearest_rank(sent, 500), "p99_sent": nearest_rank(sent, 990), "p999_sent": nearest_rank(sent, 999),
        "p50_true": nearest_rank(true, 500), "p99_true": nearest_rank(true, 990), "p999_true": nearest_rank(true, 999),
        "mean_true": sum(true) / len(true),
    }
widget.how: Seven hidden tests read latencies.csv. Percentiles must equal the expected value, and the mean is accepted within 0.001.

hints.text: Compute two lists: done minus sent, and done minus intended.
Sort each, and take the value at rank $\lceil p n / 100 \rceil$, counting from 1.
Use integers for the rank: `-(-permille * n // 1000)`. Then average the true list.

feedback.correct: That's it. Two clocks, the same sorted ranks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: The starter reads only done minus sent, and returns the middle value for every percentile. The fix builds both lists and takes the nearest rank in each. The true list has the 50 ms stall inside it, which is why its p99 is 48,821 µs.

screens.title: Quote the mean or the tail
screens.prose: A service has a mean of 19.9 µs and a p99.9 of 1,000 µs. A trader asks how fast it is.
screens.question: Which do you quote?

options.text: Both, quoting the tail first
The mean: it is the typical case
options.why: No request took 19.9 µs. The mean describes none of them.

options.text: The median only, since it ignores outliers
options.why: The median ignores exactly the requests the trader cares about.

options.text: Only the maximum, the worst case
options.why: One worst value can be a fluke. The percentiles show how often it happens.

hints.text: Who is hurt by a 1,000 µs reply?
A trader loses on the slow replies, not on the average.
Give the tail first, then the mean for the throughput picture.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does the trader lose on?

byKey.mean: The mean of 19.9 µs hides the 1,000 µs replies.
byKey.median: The median hides the tail, which is the risk.
byKey.max: A maximum alone says nothing about how often.

explain.text: The mean is a total divided by a count, and a few slow requests move it little. A trader loses on the slow ones, so quote the tail first with its percentile. The mean still helps for sizing capacity.

explain.text: The exact rank is 999, a 10 µs request, but the double 999.0000000000001 rounds up to 1,000. NumPy 2.0.2 with `inverted_cdf` does the same. Work in integers, or subtract 1e-9 before the `ceil`.

Each one as a 50 ms request, in full
options.why: It did not send them, so it never timed their wait.

options.text: Half of them, as slow requests
options.why: Closed-loop timing records none of the waiting, not half.

options.text: Only the mean, and the tail stays clean
options.why: Percentiles are unaffected too, which is the problem.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does the client send the next request?

byKey.all: The client was blocked, so it never started those requests.
byKey.half: There is no half. The wait goes unrecorded.

explain.text: The client waits for the slow reply, so the requests due meanwhile are never sent on time. It times each one from its late send. The stall appears as a single slow request.
